#881. Washington Spirit v Kansas City Current: where the NWSL Championship will be won and lost

Croix Bethune, Trinity Rodman and the Rowdy Audi crowd are among the factors that could swing Saturday’s final

This year’s NWSL Championship blends recurring themes with some newness. For the familiar: the Washington Spirit are in the final for the third straight year, hoping the third time’s the charm after back-to-back 1-0 defeats in their past two attempts. Slightly familiar, too, is Kansas City Current playing the championship game at Washington’s Audi Field, where they lost the final to Portland in 2022 and where they will contend again Saturday.

For the novelty? Neither Kansas City nor Washington, despite their modern dominance in the NWSL table, have won the championship since 2021 (when Washington won). With Gotham’s bid for a two-peat stymied by the Current in the semi-final, here are five things that will decide a new winner in 2026.

Washington’s defensive pressure Washington have allowed the second-fewest goals in the NWSL this year. Through the season and into the playoffs, the center-back pairing of the English defender Esme Morgan and Tara Rudd, the Scottish goalkeeper Sandy MacIver (fourth-highest save percentage in NWSL) and the defensive midfielder Andi Sullivan have been tough to break through for even the league’s most elite attackers. Further up the field, the Spirit’s defense begins with an attacking unit fond of forcing mistakes that lead to goals, with the late-season addition of Clara Luvanga (who has seven goal contributions in seven games for the Spirit) a key impact.

Kansas City, who have scored more goals than any other NWSL team this year, will be a challenge. Defending set pieces will be a space to watch, as they provided the only goal Utah scored against the Spirit in the semi-final, and all the goals Kansas City scored against Gotham.

Bethune on a mission against former team This season’s Midfielder of the Year is representing a team in the NWSL Championship for the third straight year (her second with availability to play). But this will be her first not representing the Spirit. After leaving Washington for Missouri in February, Bethune is facing her former team for the chance to win her first championship trophy.

A bit more poetry: Bethune nearly broke the NWSL’s all-time single-season assists record during her 2024 rookie season for the Spirit. (A torn meniscus cut short her streak, but she still was named Rookie of the Year.) She finally broke it this season with Kansas City. Her creative influence in the Current’s midfield has been crucial to unlocking their goal-scoring capabilities. Bethune’s ability to pull apart Washington’s laudable defensive structure could prove crucial in the final.

Kansas City’s attacking depth Temwa Chawinga is a two-time NWSL MVP for a reason, but she wasn’t the sole source of Kansas City’s 54 goals in 30 regular season games. The Current’s past nine goals (across five games including the playoffs) were scored by six different players, with Haley Hopkins (tied with Chawinga for goal contributions in the regular season) notching four of them. Chawinga enters the Championship with only one goal contribution in five games and no goals since 3 October, but she can break through at any moment. If not, the Current’s surrounding cast of contributors – Hopkins, Michelle Cooper, Bethune and Debinha – seems prepared to make the difference.

Rodman is the Spirit’s gamechanger The Spirit also have attacking depth, but Rodman is a gamechanger whose impact is more lopsided. Her 20 goal contributions in the regular season were more than double the goal contributions of any teammate, and that’s without quantifying the space she frees up for fellow goalscorers with her calculated off-the-ball movements.

In the postseason, Rodman has four goal contributions in two games – two goals and two assists. Coming at the end of one of her best club seasons, a big performance in the final will be essential for a Spirit victory. It would also further solidify her as one of the deserved main characters (and highest-paid player) in the NWSL.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Will Rowdy Audi make a difference? Stadium squabbles were an unexpected storyline of this year’s postseason. Gotham and Washington faced scheduling hurdles that called into question their home-field advantage and/or forced them to play on less-than-ideal pitches for their semi-finals. But this Saturday, the Spirit will still have home-field advantage at Audi Field, where they’ve earned the trust of a robust home crowd. Whether Washington can turn that familiar, friendly space into the perfect scene for actually lifting the trophy in their third straight final would be a poetic end to the postseason’s stadium woes.

#880. How to make AI data centres more sustainable

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

AI companies must engage with those who oppose the expansion of data centres.Credit: Michael M. Santiago/Getty

Around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence. Communities worry that existing infrastructure will not be able to handle the surge in demand for electricity and water, and that data centres’ energy demands will cause environmental and health problems, including increases in air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. The question of whether AI is going to stall climate action is explored in the first of a three-part Nature Podcast (Nature https://doi.org/rzqs; 2026).

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs. Where energy is concerned, however, any added demand for computing power can, and must, be met in smart, sustainable ways, not by burning more fossil fuels. Achieving this will take some creative thinking, and researchers need to be closely involved. Many argue that there are alternatives to relying on energy-intensive data centres, such as AI models that can run on individual computers or institutional servers, thereby consuming much less power than those run using cloud services. Efforts to develop such options need to be better funded.

Future projections of data centres’ energy demands are hard to make, because they are based on assumptions that could change. If current global trends continue, electricity consumption by data centres will go on rising. Between 2017 and 2024, it grew by around 12% per year. Figures for 2024 from the International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, show most of this demand coming from three regions: the United States (45%), China (25%) and Europe (15%).

The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit organization in Palo Alto, California, has projected that the continued growth of US data centres could add up to 94 gigawatts of demand by 2030, equivalent to 17% of the country’s electricity consumption. Data centres currently consume more than 1.5% of the world’s electricity supply, and the IEA’s projections indicate that this figure will more than double in the next few years. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than Japan, the agency says.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

There are serious concerns that this extra demand will be powered mainly by fossil fuels, when carbon emissions are already at a record high. Research published this week in Nature Sustainability estimates that some 400 data centres in the United States accounted for around 26 megatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, more than those produced by many countries (G. Guidi et al. Nature Sustain. https://doi.org/hcsptc; 2026). And according to a study published last week in Nature Climate Change, data centres’ energy demands could prolong the lifespan of coal-fired power stations (C. Li et al. Nature Clim. Change https://doi.org/rzqr; 2026).

But none of this is inevitable. Governments could mandate that new energy demand be met with renewable sources. And regulators could look at alternative ways to manage existing electric supplies.

Many nations’ electric grid systems are designed to accommodate surges in demand, whether to power extra cooling on hot summer days or extra heating during winter cold snaps. Much of the time, there is excess capacity. This excess could be used to reduce the amount of new energy needed to power data centres.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

One solution is to curtail data-centre operations during periods of peak electricity consumption, and ramp up at times of lower demand. An analysis released in 2025 by researchers at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, found that the US electric grid could accommodate 98 gigawatts of extra demand in this way, without adding any new generation capacity (see go.nature.com/4cdeknm). That 98 gigawatts would be enough to cover most, if not all, of the expected expansion in US data centres over the next few years.

There is potential for this to become a reality. In June, as part of a larger effort to modernize the grid, the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission instructed grid operators to draw up a plan for how they will cope with extra demand from data centres. The technology industry is understandably paying close attention to how it might mitigate the problems of powering data centres. Earlier this month, OpenAI announced what it is calling a “grid protectors program”, a project to consult with US grid operators, regulators and policymakers to see how the company can work around peaks in power demand.

Meanwhile, Google is paying households and businesses in parts of the Eastern United States to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Similar proposals are being considered in other countries.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

These are all tentative moves in the right direction, although arguably progress is not being made fast enough. Policymakers and data-centre operators must engage seriously with those who oppose the centres’ expansion. At a minimum, any new energy sources developed to power these centres must be renewable. Existing energy sources can also be better deployed, and researchers working to develop alternatives to energy-intensive data centres should be better supported. More peer-reviewed evidence is needed, especially for countries outside the United States.

There are smarter and more sustainable ways to power the growth of AI, but to achieve them, concerted and coordinated action will be needed. In this way, the harm posed to people and the planet can be minimized, and AI technologies can benefit everyone.

#878. Summer signings join Lionel Messi among MLS’s top earners: Takeaways from the league’s salary release

How much in player salaries did it take to earn a point in the 2026 MLS regular season? The latest batch of salaries lends some insight

Lionel Messi has closer company at the top of MLS’s list of highest-paid players, thanks to another pair of former Barcelona attackers. The Inter Miami captain is still comfortably the league’s top earner, on a guaranteed compensation of $28.3m. Robert Lewandowski (Chicago Fire) and Antoine Griezmann (Orlando City) have entered the list with the second and third highest wages, while Atlanta United’s Breel Embolo, another summer signing, ranks fifth on a guaranteed compensation of $10.8m. Second-year LAFC forward Son Heung-min sits fourth on $11.2m.

Casimiro, who joined Messi in Miami at the end of his contract with Manchester United, is his team’s fourth top-earner with a guaranteed compensation of $3.54m. This comes after Miami announced his signing as a non-designated player to the surprise of some as the Brazilian arrived on a Bosman transfer rather than a loan-with-purchase, as Rodrigo De Paul had last summer, to keep Miami rules compliant. The MLS Players’ Association lists Casimiro on a base salary of $896,004.

All of these earnings figures were revealed as part of the MLS Players’ Association’s twice-a-year data dump, with the latter installment dropping hours before the league’s postseason commenced. While these figures don’t include transfer fees and therefore don’t tell the whole picture of a team’s investment in its roster, it’s a useful bit of insight in regards to how each team is spending on player wages.

Figures are players’ guaranteed compensation inclusive of base salary and all guaranteed bonuses; does not include marketing and other bonuses.

Thirteen of MLS’s 30 clubs have a new highest earner after a busy post-World Cup transfer window. Two – Anders Dreyer (San Diego, $3.6m) and Mateusz Bogusz (Houston, $2.5m) – rose to the top after the departure of a higher-paid teammate. Lozano overtook the injured Riqui Puig after arriving with the LA Galaxy on loan from San Diego. Lewandowski, Griezmann, and Embolo hold similar status, while Charlotte replaced Wilfried Zaha with Allan Saint-Maximin ($7.2m) earning nearly three times as much as the Crystal Palace great.

Other top-earners signed from beyond the league are Brais Méndez (Columbus, $5.2m), André Luiz (Kansas City, $3.3m), and Kai Wagner (Philadelphia, $1.6m). Two strikers who were traded within the league mid-season signed fresh terms that made them their new teams’ highest-paid players: Rafael Navarro (St. Louis, $4.95m) and Dejan Joveljic (Seattle, $3.7m).

The standout failure of the new big earners is Alexis Sánchez. The 37-year-old Chile legend came to North America this summer, joining CF Montréal and making 15 league appearances for the Quebecois club but failing to register a single goal or assist. His $2.97m guaranteed compensation makes up 24.6% of the team’s wage bill.

Griezmann’s arrival means that Messi no longer carries the largest share of any team’s wage bill, as Orlando has dedicated slightly more to the Frenchman (49.5%) than Miami has to the Argentinian (47.7%). Lewandowski narrowly trails by accounting for 47.3% of Chicago’s wage spending. Importantly, Messi’s contract includes add-ons; a portion of Apple TV subscriptions, merchandise sales through Adidas and Fanatics, and an optional ownership stake in Miami when he retires.

Other notable new wages include former Middlesbrough attacking midfielder Morgan Whittaker (Colorado, $2.0m), former Watford and Everton midfielder Abdoulaye Doucouré (Charlotte, $1.0m), former Manchester United left-back Tyrell Malacia (Cincinnati, $1.04m), former NYCFC playmaker Santi Rodríguez (Columbus, $3.9m), South Africa striker Lyle Foster (Houston, $1.8m), former Celtic striker Kyōgo Furuhashi (LA Galaxy, $1.1m), Tunisia winger Elias Saad (Nashville, $1.7m), former Leeds winger Jack Harrison (New England, $3.65m), Côte d’Ivoire winger Bénie Traoré (NYCFC, $2.5m), former Netherlands striker Vincent Janssen (Portland, $1.75m), Tunisia winger Elias Achouri (San Diego, $2.6m), Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn (San Jose, $1.6m), and Southampton loanee Damion Downs (St Louis, $1.6m).

While this exercise cannot confidently include every transfer fee paid, the timing of this year’s drop after the regular season’s end allows us to size up how teams spent on wages against the league table.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Does spending more equal success? There’s a degree of correlation there, but it’s not strong.

#876. Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support

More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for possible reparations.

"We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation.

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression," wrote the signatories of the appeal.

The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English.

While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made.

"Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters."

The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades.

Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution.

However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions.

When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS)  made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022.

The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution.

In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland."

"Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23.

Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture."

"Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw.

"Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance.

The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros.

To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW.

The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die."

Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture."

"It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka.

This article was originally written in German.

#875. The four 'what next?' scenarios for Premier League after Man City ruling

Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City

If you had the impression that the saga over Manchester City's 115 charges was almost over, think again.

Two years since the hearing began, the Premier League has confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of its financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and would pursue "appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."

It appears the chaos and uncertainty is only going to increase now.

City fans, and the rest of football, are left to guess what the punishment might be. And when this all might reach a definitive conclusion.

The charges are so serious that some form of points deduction now appears inevitable, subject to the appeal by City, who strongly refute the accusations.

When and how any punishment is applied will be crucial not just for City, but the Premier League as a whole.

And that's before we get to the prospect of clubs suing City for compensation.

Enzo Maresca's side go to Liverpool on 11 October when the Premier League resumes after the international break. They could go six points clear at the top. But is that now rendered meaningless?

Let's look at possible scenarios - none of which are particularly appealing.

No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains

Deciding the punishment should be quicker than ascertaining guilt, but nothing is certain in this case.

As the charges have been denied, it will have to go to a sanction hearing convened by the independent panel.

At the hearing, everything will be on the table. Fines, points deductions and even demotion.

This differs from Chelsea's case earlier this year, as the Stamford Bridge club self-reported and admitted guilt. That allowed them to negotiate with the Premier League and reach a sanctioning agreement.

The panel will have to comb through the hundreds of pages of evidence and determine the punishment.

Remember, Everton were docked six points, reduced from 10 on appeal, and then two points in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR). Nottingham Forest were deducted four points.

These were considered to be minor breaches, while City faced seven separate charges on PSR breaches in the Premier League alone, as well as a further five related to Uefa competitions.

This aspect alone suggests a large points penalty.

That is before you get into the findings that the club arranged "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs", equating to roughly Â£830m of extra revenue from sponsorship deals.

Take all this into account, and it places an asterisk against the Premier League between 2009 and 2018.

Chelsea and Manchester City, two of the competition's most successful clubs, have been part of that. While Chelsea admitted effectively cheating, City have been found guilty. They got around the financial rules to put them in a position to be able to sign more expensive players than their finances should have permitted.

And if this season passes with no decision on the sanction while it is known City were guilty of the majority of counts, what does that mean for the integrity of the competition?

Could a penalty be backdated to this season when finally awarded? Unlikely.

So what if Manchester City win the league?

Coventry are third from bottom right now. What if they finish in that position, are relegated, but would have stayed up had City's punishment come this season?

This inertia is terrible news for the Premier League as a competition.

There's a strong argument that a sanctioning agreement is the cleanest way out of this.

But that may not be palatable to the league as they would have to negotiate with City, who would presumably want a lesser punishment.

Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation

Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict

Man City legal fight could spiral out of control - Purslow

The usual process when any points penalty is handed down is that it is applied immediately, subject to appeal.

It could be a points deduction so large that it is effectively a relegation.

Alternatively, if City's membership of the Premier League was revoked, it is unclear how that might be applied mid-season.

It could also be that the punishment is a huge fine, although that would seem unlikely given points deductions to other clubs.

The question would be how soon we hear, and how long after the appeal is heard.

While there are timelines for the appeal process within the Premier League regulations, it is unclear whether they would directly apply here.

Usually, the league asks for an expedited process from the independent arbitration company which handles disciplinary cases.

But, as ever in this case, the complexities indicate this is not straightforward.

There is the chance, though slim, that the punishment is only applied to the league table after the appeal.

That would surely lead to protests from impacted teams this season, who will demand it should, as usual, come into effect immediately.

For the integrity of the Premier League, so all clubs know what they are playing for, this would need to happen sooner rather than later.

Last season, a points deduction for West Bromwich Albion related to breaches of profit and sustainability regulations was not announced until 24 April.

While ultimately they stayed in the Championship, it plunged them back into a relegation fight when they thought they were safe. It also gave some hope to the teams in the relegation zone.

The Premier League does not want this to drag on until the penultimate month of the season, but nothing is guaranteed in this story.

In this scenario, let's not forget City could also win their appeal, like they did over a two-year Champions League ban handed down by Uefa in July 2020.

However, unlike with Uefa, City would not be able to take this case to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

While this would be celebrated at Etihad Stadium it would likely not be the end of the acrimony over the case.

Manchester City won seven domestic trophies during the period of the alleged offences

Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation from Manchester City over the case.

One source, who held a senior executive position at two Premier League sides, said they expected clubs to submit individual compensation claims against Manchester City.

Another leading lawyer told the BBC that process could even be centralised by the league.

Premier League rules allow clubs to seek legal action against each other for compensation.

In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley Â£35m after they broke PSR over a three-year period.

Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.

Everton are appealing, with sources previously saying they would "robustly and thoroughly" contest the ruling, but it provides an interesting backdrop to the Manchester City case.

There is uncertainty over a statute of limitations, which would set a cut-off point for claims.

Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham Hotspur reportedly preserved their rights to claim compensation two years ago.

This is not just about Manchester United (twice) and Liverpool, who finished as runners-up to City in their title-winning seasons.

It is about those clubs who just missed out on the Champions League, or failed to make Europe, or even those who were relegated.

And it could even result in claims over the prize money for each Premier League place, or the potential commercial earnings lost by rival clubs.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport it would be considered a "denial of an opportunity" by complainants.

Maguire explained that the "statute of limitations is not referenced" in the Premier League's traditional handbook, though that could be subject to a legal challenge from City.

But what of the compensation? Just looking at Champions League qualifying could bring huge financial claims.

"The Champions League in those days was worth a minimum of Â£30m," Maguire said. "I think by the time we got to 2018, it was probably worth Â£60m or Â£70m, and that's in prize money.

"On top of that, you could claim for loss of gate receipts, loss of sponsor bonuses. This is highly unlikely, but it's certainly being discussed.

"Players get bonuses for qualifying for the Champions League. Those bonuses, if you talk to people connected to the elite clubs, are normally in the region of 25%.

"An average salary in those days would probably, if you go back to 2012, be in the region of Â£80,000 or Â£90,000 a week. Twenty-five percent of that is four or five million pounds a year. That's how the issues stack up."

Points deductions, fines, and compensation claims.

This is an extremely messy situation for the Premier League, and it does not look like being resolved anytime soon.

#874. Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’

A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty

In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.

Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.

Scared, exhausted and running on adrenaline, the team had lived through another episode of disruption; but in truth they had rarely known stability. For Syrian women’s footballers, navigating uncertainty had been part of the game long before the country’s political upheaval reached its latest turning point. “My generation was burned away and completely lost,” said Noor Jumaa, a former national team goalkeeper. “It was like everything that was being built just disappeared.”

After 14 years of war, Syria has much to rebuild. Women’s football is among the institutions trying to recover from a conflict that erased an entire generation of players, interrupted the development of the game itself and left its infrastructure struggling. Yet, in recent years, Syria’s youth teams have emerged as one of the country’s more unexpected sporting success stories, winning regional titles and producing players who are beginning to make their mark abroad.

Syria’s women’s national team played their first international match in 2005. By 2011, plans were under way for an 11-a-side women’s league. Then the uprising began, and all plans were abandoned. For the next six years, women’s football in Syria effectively stopped. There were no international fixtures at any level, only occasional futsal tournaments. More than six million people eventually fled Syria, including hundreds involved in the sport, leaving an already small pool of players scattered across the world.

Men’s football, by contrast, continued. The national team played matches abroad after Syria was barred from hosting fixtures in 2011 on security grounds. The Assad regime used its successes to project an image of normality, even welcoming the squad to his palace after their 2012 WAFF Championship victory. Fifa, despite its rules against political interference, stayed silent.

Girls growing up in those years had no women’s team to watch. “I was watching a match of Syria’s men’s national team, and I was really upset. I would say, ‘God, if only they’d make a national team for girls,’” recalled Raneem Abo Lateef, a 21-year-old goalkeeper for Syria. The opportunity came unexpectedly after her family moved houses, and a girl next door told Abo Lateef that a relative was starting a girls’ club. “Girls’ football? Wow,” she said. “It was like dreams coming true.”

Similarly, international teammate Julnar Mustafa spent hours playing with boys in her neighbourhood in Hasakah. Born in 2008, so too young to remember the beginning of the uprising, she filmed herself dribbling and performing tricks on her phone, uploading the videos to Facebook. A regional coach came across them and invited Mustafa to join his team.

But finding an opportunity to play was only part of the challenge. “In our society, especially in the north, in Hasakah, sport is completely off-limits for girls,” Mustafa told the Guardian. “Not football, not anything”.

While a new generation of girls were finding their way into football, the national team was attempting to return to international competition. In April 2017, Syria entered the Asian Cup qualifiers in Vietnam, assembling a squad after six years without any activity. The federation announced tryouts on Facebook, and players were given about a month of preparation. Syria went on to lose every match, including a 14-0 defeat by Myanmar. “Honestly, it was one of the worst teams in Syria’s history,” said Jumaa, who was part of that squad. “We lost by terrifying scores.”

Maha Al-Katreb, also in the squad at the time, remembers the criticism that followed. Players were ridiculed despite having had little preparation. At the tournament, she saw opponents arrive with larger coaching staffs and younger players training alongside their senior teams. The gap between Syria and their regional competitors was difficult to ignore.

With injuries ending her career early, Al-Katreb fell into coaching by chance and turned towards building a programme that could develop the next generation. She later joined the Syrian Football Association (SFA), taking on administrative and coaching responsibilities.

A six-team women’s senior league was established in 2019, followed by the development of youth national teams. This year the country held an inaugural edition of its youth league. Al-Katreb developed Syria’s first women’s football strategy, submitted to Fifa, that set out a longer-term plan for expanding participation and creating a pathway into the national teams. “You have to start building from the bottom if you want to see results after these 10 years,” Al-Katreb said. “So that we don’t burn one generation after another.”

In 2022, women accounted for only 1,000 of Syria’s 25,000 registered footballers. The women’s football strategy, seen by the Guardian, aimed to increase female participation by 150% over four years, including through 33 school training centres across 11 provinces, with capacity for 1,650 girls by 2026.

The government has also outlined plans to rehabilitate the country’s sporting infrastructure. Rami Alsubea, an adviser at the Ministry of Sport and Youth, said in a statement that 48 sports facilities had been rehabilitated in 2025, with plans to rehabilitate about 150 more and build about 20 new ones by 2028. Restoring infrastructure is in part to meet hosting criteria set by Fifa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Al-Katreb left the federation more than a year ago. Jumaa is now part of a two-woman team leading its women’s football department, appointed after the arrival of the federation’s current president, Feras al-Teet. Several players have criticized the federation’s leadership and the pace of progress. The Guardian reached out to Al-Teet for comment. He declined.

Among the players who have been vocal about the shortcomings is 26-year-old Rona Aizouk, one of the most experienced members of the current generation. Named after Brazilian footballer Ronaldinho, she made history in 2023 when she became the first Syrian-born woman to sign a professional contract, joining Saudi side Najmat Jeddah. Her performances in Syria had attracted the club’s attention, but securing the move proved difficult. Visa refusals and paperwork complications delayed her arrival until two days before the season began. Her time in Saudi Arabia lasted only a few months, and she was unable to extend her stay.

“Honestly, I went there not wanting to come back,” said Aizouk. “There’s no comparison. Everything is better, the treatment, the training, the facilities. It’s just different.

“The most important thing is the players’ comfort. Here in Syria, we have to endure psychological pressure and torment. As a player, I have to fight the world just to achieve even a little bit of success.”

After returning to Damascus to complete her studies, Aizouk quickly received interest from multiple clubs in Jordan, where she now plays. For her, being in situ abroad is about more than personal progression. “I want to be a message that I, who came out of hard circumstances and out of a war, still managed to succeed.”

Aizouk’s exposure to regional excellence has shown her that Syria is still many years behind. At the forefront is financial restriction that has left the sport bare-boned. International sanctions and banking restrictions imposed on Syria left millions of dollars in development funding from Fifa inaccessible to the SFA, preventing it from fully benefiting from programmes such as Fifa Forward.

Although broad economic sanctions have since been lifted, an estimated $11.5m in funds remains inaccessible to the federation. Both the SFA and Fifa insist they are working to establish a mechanism through which the money can be transferred. For now, the support has been seen in training equipment.

The financial strain is felt directly by players as both the national team and regional league are operated by the SFA. Clubs frequently go months without paying wages, and when payments do arrive, players say they can fall short of the amounts agreed. International call-ups offer little relief: during national team duty, including training camps, players receive a daily allowance of $20, capped at $200 for the length of their stay, regardless of how long it is. Some say the costs of travelling and playing can exceed what they receive.

Several clubs have folded since the domestic league’s launch in 2019, citing financial difficulties and the continued disruption caused by the war and ongoing conflicts. Those that remain often struggle to provide even basic resources.

Al-Hilal, now renamed Qamishlo Sport, have become one of the country’s most successful women’s sides, currently reigning as senior and youth league champions. But their achievements have not translated into financial security, according to head coach, Daleel Khalid. “There’s an absence of adequate support from all sides and the parties responsible for Syrian women’s sports, whether in terms of training camps and preparation, or the capabilities and infrastructure needed to develop the game,” he said.

The club’s campaign at the 2026 WAFF Women’s Clubs Championship was a big test. The tournament brought together league champions from six regional competitions. Despite having only a short training camp at home, Al-Hilal reached the final against Saudi champions Al-Nassr. Abo Lateef and Mustafa were among those who represented them, and their performances offered a reminder that Syrian teams can compete with the region’s best, even when their opponents have considerably greater resources.

There was also individual recognition. Al-Hilal’s Mai Al-Jani was named the tournament’s best player after a series of standout performances, an achievement she was quick to share with those around her. “The award I won is a source of pride for me, for the club and for the players. I see it as a team award,” she said. “It belongs to the staff, the players, and every Syrian girl living through these difficult circumstances.”

Born in 2006 in a small village in Homs province, Al-Jani has emerged as one of Syria’s promising attacking talents. She won the league’s Golden Boot in the 2024-25 season and has continued to impress for both club and country. She was also named the best player at the 2023 WAFF under-17 championship, when Syria won their first international title in women’s football. Al-Katreb, who was an assistant coach, saw the victory as evidence of what the country could build with the right support.

The WAFF under-17 triumph was repeated at the 2026 edition with a completely different squad. “It was joy that everyone in the country needed,” said Jumaa. “We were completely outnumbered in technical and admin staff, with only nine of us managing everything. Other teams had double the number of staff, with gameplay technology we can’t get our hands on.”

For Abo Lateef, the greatest risk is allowing another generation of players to lose the chance to compete. The senior women’s national team, for instance, has not played in over two years, with no reason given to players. “We need competition, regardless of the level,” said Abo Lateef. “I’m afraid a day will come when I’m made to sit at home, as was the case with the ones before us. A friendly fixture is a good start. Anything.”

Aizouk’s message to those responsible for the future of the women’s game was more direct. “Save Syrian football,” she said. “Save the generations. Save us.”

#873. 'Why not have a go?' - the halfway line goal phenomenon

Diego Gomez's shot against Crystal Palace soars over Walter Benitez

David Beckham's goal from the halfway line against Wimbledon in 1996 is one of football's iconic moments.

It helped to catapult the Manchester United midfielder to global stardom and remains a staple of highlight reels.

The impudence to shoot from such a distance highlighted the exceptional talent and character of the future England captain.

Premier League players are now trying their luck from long range more regularly, testing their instinct, precision and technique.

Diego Gomez's stunning 51-metre (56-yard) strike for Brighton against Crystal Palace last month added to the spectacular list in the Premier League, while players in the EFL and FA Cup have contributed their own.

There have already been 19 attempts from over 50 metres this season, on course to beat last season's Premier League total of 26.

Of the 2,733 shots in the Premier League this term, 0.7% of them have come from over halfway - up on 0.3% over the course of last season.

This sample size is admittedly small. And in the case of goals scored from distance lower down the football pyramid, this is data that isn't readily available.

But why are we seeing a growing number of shots being taken from such extravagant distance?

Gomez tried to score from deep in his own half during Brighton's 2-0 win at Sunderland on 10 October.

A week later, he beat Walter Benitez with the longest-range goal in the Premier League since Wayne Rooney's 57.6m strike for Everton against West Ham in 2017.

The Paraguayan took advice from Lionel Messi, when the pair were at Inter Miami, to always look to play the ball forward to another level.

It is not just Premier League players who are trying their luck from outrageous distances.

Charlie McNeill scored from halfway for Crewe in their recent 2-1 FA Cup win against AFC Wimbledon.

The on-loan Sheffield Wednesday forward, who played once for Manchester United before leaving Old Trafford in 2024, beat goalkeeper Joe Bursik to open the scoring.

Having done it while at Manchester City and Manchester United's academies, the 23-year-old felt his latest attempt was instinctive.

He told BBC Sport: "Goalies nowadays are always quite high up the pitch - playing a sweeper-keeper role - and I always have a thought if I ever got into that situation to have a go.

"You see it more and more. I had the opportunity so I thought: 'Why not have a go?'

"It was one of those goals. I turned and saw him off his line and in that split-second made the decision to shoot.

"I knew I caught it sweetly and I was following it the whole way in so I knew it had a good chance, but as the keeper was going back I thought he was going to get it.

"When I watched it back it dropped quite early, but as it was getting closer and closer I thought it was going to go over because it went quite high but it dropped in."

Crewe Alexandra's Charlie McNeill talking about the rise in halfway line goals

McNeill joins a growing number of players to have scored from the halfway line or inside their own half over the past 18 months.

Preston Fearon, now on loan at Forest Green, scored two goals from around the halfway line for West Ham Under-21s in their win against Burnley last month.

Gbemi Arubi was barely a stride over the halfway line when he scored for Burton against Peterborough in October.

Last season, Abdul Fatawu (Leicester), Ryan Ledson (Huddersfield), Reyes Cleary (Barnsley), Regan Hendry (Mansfield) and Sammy Braybrooke (Newport) all scored from the halfway line or inside their own half in the EFL.

Two years ago, Chelsea's Moises Caicedo scored from the centre circle against Bournemouth.

Is it all about the goalkeeper's position, as they stand higher up the pitch to either stop opposition attacks or get their own team moving?

"You've got to execute it properly, but it plays a big part. Most keepers are like that, high out the net, because we are playing over the top so they are there first, to get the ball," said McNeill.

"I have always had it in my head and have tried it a couple of times. Although it's not like I do my homework and see he is always off his line. It's one of those instinctive moments."

Paul Robinson scored two goals in his career, one for Tottenham and one for Leeds

Asmir Begovic holds the record for the longest-range Premier League goal when the goalkeeper scored from 95.7m for Stoke against Southampton in 2013.

Two other goalkeepers have scored from their own half: Tim Howard for Everton against Bolton in 2012 and Paul Robinson, who netted for Tottenham against Watford in 2007.

Yet they were flukes rather than by design - similar to Barrow goalkeeper Ben Winterbottom's goal from his own half in their 3-0 National League win at Gateshead on Saturday.

Robinson, who also scored for Leeds against Swindon in 2004, external, feels conceding from distance is now a risk managers are willing to take.

The former England international said: "We've seen the game evolve in the way where the goalkeeper becomes a key figure in starting a pattern of play. The manager wants the goalkeeper at the base of the back three, four or five.

"But then also we're seeing a lot more teams playing with a higher line and the goalkeeper then has to take a higher line of starting position to read the through ball.

"When your team are playing a high line, you obviously have to be further up the field and you're concentrating on where your defensive line is, as opposed to where the football is at times.

"It's one of those things modern-day managers are willing to accept if and when it does happen, because of the way they want their goalkeeper to play.

"We see so many managers come out now and say: 'It's OK. I'm quite happy with them making mistakes. This is the way I want them to play. Blame me because that's what I've asked them to do.'

"We're probably entering that type of territory with it."

With attackers aware of the higher starting position of opposing keepers - a result of teams pressing high - and likely to have been encouraged by the success of other long-range efforts across football, attempts from extreme distance are becoming more frequent in the Premier League this season.

The conversion of efforts from more than 50 metres have increased too - up to 5.3% this season, compared to 1.1% across the previous three seasons combined, with Gomez's strike the first Premier League goal scored from over 50 metres since the 2023-24 season.

It's a small sample size, so more time is required for clearer trends, at least in the Premier League to be established.

But with more long shots being taken and keepers starting higher, there is a suggestion (and hope) we may see more Goal of the Season contenders before the term is out.

#872. Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden

The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly

It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.

But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakably Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan, Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio. From one of the absolute greats.

Danny died last week. In a beautiful tribute on the Spurs podcast he hosted – A View From the Lane – Charlie Eccleshare pointed out the irony that for someone so articulate and erudite and able to do so much more than just “the football”, his most iconic moment is so simple. Even the opening noise – not even a real word – is perfect in that context.

Terms such as pioneer and trailblazer often get thrown out in moments like this. But Danny really was. I first met him at BBC London more than 20 years ago. As someone who’d listened to him and Danny Baker as a teenager, I couldn’t really believe I was in the same office as them. His career was ridiculous, editing the NME and Q magazine, setting up Football365, but it was radio where I knew him. He understood the absurdity of life and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living by talking about football. I remember at TalkSport one World Cup – 2018 perhaps – wandering in and he was hosting a live match, watching a game on the TV just marvelling at the fact that this was a job, and that this was his job.

And he was funny. Blimey he was funny – what an ability to be blessed with. I listened to a best of Baker and Kelly Upfront from the old Radio 5 on YouTube the other day; amazing calls about Arthur Cox locking a disgruntled fan in his office for two and a half hours, a man playing football with a pig’s head in a sausage factory in Peckham: “I used to like the volleys when the eyes popped out.” Anyone who has tried to make funny football content, of any kind – radio, TV, podcasts, social media – owes him a debt of gratitude.

Last Wednesday Charlie Baker and I had to try to do him justice on TalkSport. Afternoon UK time, midnight till 3am for me in Australia. I was asleep when my phone rang and instantly presumed I’d slept through my alarm and missed the show. A millisecond of internal panic surged through me as I jumped up and cracked a shin on the bedside table. Danny would appreciate the ridiculous scene of me hopping around in the dark trying not to wake the kids while one of the bosses gave me the incredibly sad news.

If you’ve broadcast for any amount of time, you will be confronted with having to host shows just after someone has died. Jack Charlton, Terry Venables, Jimmy Greaves – but never before have I had to pay tribute to a friend.

Paul Hawksbee’s voice cracks and we all go. There are West Ham and Chelsea fans calling admitting they listen to his Spurs podcast because it’s him. There are all manner of texts recounting hilarious stories they heard on his shows over the last 30 years: the man who took a TV to a game in Northern Ireland so they could watch the FA Cup final, having to move around holding the aerial to keep the signal.

There’s a moment I think Danny would have found so funny, when I’m being sad – because it is sad, and I am sad – and into the break I read the sponsor’s lines: “This show is brought to you by Toolstation, first stop Toolstation” in such a maudlin way it’s as if I’m delivering a eulogy, just one sponsored by a hardware store. I catch myself just in time.

But, most important, there are so many messages from people who never met Danny, who never knew him, but who felt as if they knew him. We believed he would have wanted a bit of fuss made of him.

He definitely knew the enduring power of radio, even as the broadcasting landscape changes so quickly. It connects in a way nothing else can. And nothing said that more than messages we received from listeners who at one time or another were struggling and going through incredibly hard times and Danny’s energy, wit and joy were an escape and a tonic.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There will be a million people more important in Danny’s life than me. Our paths crossed a great deal, but never for very long. I was a minuscule cog in his world – but Danny had so much love to give. Voice notes about how to broadcast remotely or celebrating Spurs’ win in Bilbao; the tributes showed he had almost infinite time for others.

It always feels such a bland cliche to say it’s impossible to consider someone so full of life not being there – we all know we have a sell-by date. At the start of October he had been given a choice: to ebb away slowly over a couple of years or have a big but very risky operation. Danny never ebbed.

He sent a big group WhatsApp voice note to many friends and colleagues, and I don’t think he would mind me writing what it said.

“I want you to know that I’ve enjoyed being around you, I’ve learnt from you, I’ve enjoyed working with you, you know how much I love my work – the fact I’m pretty good at it is secondary to how much I enjoy it, but look I’m very much hopeful that the boffins and my own determination will get me through this and we can all laugh about this message. But know how I care about you, how much you have meant in my life and on Thursday night or Friday morning when you look at the sky or feel the wind against your face, think about me and what’s happening and hopefully we’ll all have a pint and a laugh about this somewhere down the line.”

From “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH” to that – his words just hit the right tone every time.

#871. What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?

Starship still has some work to do before it's fully up and running.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running.

The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms.

It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully, nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.

SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved.

Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company.

"That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

The Flight 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX.

And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average.

Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites. And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft, if all goes to plan.

For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment.

Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship.

The company has reflown Super Heavy vehicles on two separate occasions. Booster 14 initially launched on Flight 7 in January 2025, then lifted off again on Flight 9 in May of that year. Booster 15 flew on Flight 8 and Flight 11, which lifted off in March 2025 and October 2025, respectively.

Several months separated each of these Super Heavy reflights. And SpaceX has yet to reuse a Ship, as it had not caught one during a mission until Saturday.

That could change soon: Before Flight 15 lifted off, Musk said that the company wants to reuse both of its Starship stages. That option may still be on the table for Flight 15's Ship.

And we should expect full reuse to be a priority on Starship test flights over the longer haul, with SpaceX working toward shorter and shorter turnaround times — perhaps until an hourly cadence is in sight, if that goal is indeed achievable.

Over the next few years, most Starship launches will likely be devoted to building out the Starlink V3 and Starmind megaconstellations. But the rocket will also carry people to deep space, if all goes to plan, which will require the checking of another set of boxes.

NASA selected Ship to be the first crewed lunar lander for its Artemis program, which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole by 2032 or so. Current plans call for Ship to land astronauts in that locale for the first time on the Artemis IV mission, which is targeted to fly in 2028.

SpaceX needs to install a crew cabin and life-support system in Ship to make that happen. The company is working on that now and has made considerable progress, according to NASA. Last month, an agency presentation reported that SpaceX is on target to finish building "Cabin 1," a full-scale ground prototype of Ship's crew cabin, by the end of the year.

There's another hurdle to clear, however. On all deep-space missions, Ship will need to fill up its fuel tanks after launch, at a "depot" that SpaceX will set up in Earth orbit. (Launching Ship with full tanks is not an option, as it would be incredibly heavy in that case.)

The depot will be filled by "tanker" variants of Ship. It's unclear how many tanker visits will be required for each Ship deep-space mission; outside experts have floated numbers as high as 22, while Musk has cited six to eight as a probable range.

Whatever the actual number, Ship will need to demonstrate proficiency with off-Earth refueling, something it has yet to do. And there's more to it than just a simple rendezvous: Ship's engines run on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, so the propellants must be kept extremely cold throughout the process.

We're likely to see the first refueling test relatively soon, as time is of the essence for SpaceX. If the company can't get Ship ready for the Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, NASA may go with another private lander — Blue Origin's Blue Moon, which the agency also contracted for Artemis missions.

All of this is to say that, while Flight 15 was a big success for Starship and SpaceX, there's a lot of work left to do — and a lot for space fans to watch for over the coming weeks and months.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#870. UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law

A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's last court of appeal.

A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in  the UK.

"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."

The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."

Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.

One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion."

Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.

Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."

He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.

"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.

The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.

The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.

The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.

Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.

But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

#869. What's the story with Scotland boss Pocognoli - is it time to go?

A few short months ago, Craig Mulholland, the Scottish FA's chief football officer, and Ian Maxwell, the association's chief executive, spoke about the worldwide search for a new Scotland head coach.

The data, the metrics, the cosmic input from the analytics company whose input was received at Hampden as if written on tablets of stone.

The process all pointed to Sebastien Pocognoli being their guy. They paraded him around Hampden, told everybody that loads of clubs were on his tail but that they won the chase.

They may, or may not, have mentioned the word 'coup' but that was certainly what their body language was telling you.

For coup, read boo, the sound surely reverberating around the Tartan Army right now after Monday's 4-0 defeat by Switzerland.

Some nonsense has been written about Pocognoli being on twice the salary that Steve Clarke was on, but whatever they're paying him, there's no value in it so far.

Money is a factor here. Clarke's three qualifications brought a rich bounty into the SFA's coffers, many millions even after deductions. That cash gave the association a little more opportunity to do some of the things they want to do in grassroots football.

A world where Scotland miss out on major championships and the financial windfalls that come with qualification is not a place they want to revisit. The next Euros looks like a gimme - almost harder not to qualify than qualify - but the sense of drift in this team is alarming and can't go on much longer.

Mulholland, Maxwell and let's throw SFA president Mike Mulraney into the mix, should be feeling mightily nervous.

Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Robertson

Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland

Robertson eclipses Dalglish to become Scotland's most capped man

Most people understood that Pocognoli needed time, but implicit in that understanding was a need to see something developing under him, a burgeoning style of play, some positives here and there, a few signs that even though things might not be great today or tomorrow, they're inching in the right direction.

There's been none of that. Decent players look lost. Pocognoli's system has made Scotland a disjointed soft touch. Structural discipline collapses too often. Players charge forward and leave space in behind. He wants hard pressing and maximum intensity, but his players don't look capable of providing it.

In six games they have scored five goals - two from the penalty spot. Promises of jam tomorrow are not cutting it. People can see a team on the slide.

In Switzerland, there was a drubbing that piles the heat on the Belgian, on the people who appointed him and on the players, too.

'You do not have time in international football'

If the chaos on the field wasn't a bad enough look for Pocognoli, then some of the words said in the wake of this objectionable 4-0 pummelling to a Switzerland B side playing in third gear only made things worse.

Andy Robertson, on the night he became Scotland's most capped player in history, delivered a damning riff that sounded strongly like a commentary on this coaching regime and this set of players.

In his stead, John McGinn did much the same thing. "You don't get time" was the gist. Who doesn't get time?

Robertson and McGinn didn't lay it on the line, but their thoughts resembled distress flares. These Scotland players can be overhyped, but they are better than some of the nonsense they dished up in St Gallen.

More than one former Scotland international reckoned they saw players not exactly busting a gut out there. These guys know the tell-tale signs.

Some private conversations between the SFA hierarchy and the senior operators in this team need to take place. What were they suggesting in the post-match? What are they really thinking?

An honesty session behind closed doors needs to take place long before the qualification campaign for the next Euros begins in March.

Pocognoli comes across as a good person: open, communicative, passionate and hard-working.

He also appears stubborn in the way he sets up his team, a system that is so easily exploited by more experienced coaches, people like Switzerland boss Murat Yakin, who was missing a battalion of heavy hitters and yet still won this game at a canter.

Yakin started six players who had six caps or fewer to their name - three of them scored.

McGinn said later that Scotland were in this movie before in the early days of Clarke's tenure, mentioning the 4-0 loss to Russia in 2019 - four goals conceded in 27 minutes.

The difference between Clarke and Pocognoli is obvious. Clarke had vast experience and the nous to fix the problems. Pocognoli is a young coach with no such back story, no such track record in turning bad situations into good.

Pocognoli said later that people should look beyond the result, to the "attitude of the players" who were at times "brilliant, brave and on the front foot".

He argued that 4-0 wasn't a true reflection of the game, referring to the glaring misses by Lewis Ferguson and Scott McTominay. Scotland were 3-0 down at the time. He didn't think the loss had anything to do with a system or a lack of confidence or a lack of belief.

Not many fans were buying what he was selling. Listening to some of his players, you doubted that they were buying it either.

After the home loss to Slovenia, Robertson said his team had been "out-played" and "out-fought." There were some other comments made after the desperately stodgy 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday. On Monday, it cranked up another level.

McGinn was asked if he felt Scotland were on the right path. "Impossible for me to say yes," he replied. It was hard to listen to what the players were trying to say and conclude that everybody's on the same page in this set-up.

Intransigence is not a good characteristic for any manager. In recent times we've seen a few bosses at big clubs who were wedded to their principles. Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy didn't last long at Rangers and Celtic.

To repeat Robertson's line, you don't get time.

Clarke had an instinctive understanding of that and pragmatism was his way of taking his team forward, difficult yard by difficult yard. Rigid idealism is not a sensible way to operate, but Pocognoli has gone down that road in his first six games.

It's a dead-end down there. He needs to turn back and find another way while he still can. If he still can.

'Scotland have not played well in any game this campaign'
